title: Surveillance Legislation Amendment (Identify and Disrupt) Bill 2021
short_title: Surveillance Legislation Amendment (Identify and Disrupt) Bill 2021

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would give the Australian Federal Police and the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission new powers to fight serious online crime.
It would create three new warrant types: data disruption, network activity, and account takeover warrants.
The bill includes sunset provisions for warrants and emergency authorisations.
changes: Introduces data disruption warrants to modify, add, copy or delete data to frustrate serious online offences.
Introduces network activity warrants to collect intelligence on criminal networks.
Introduces account takeover warrants to let agencies take control of online accounts for evidence gathering.
Adds sunset provisions for warrants and emergency authorisations.
summary.affected: The Australian Federal Police and the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission, and people suspected of serious online crime such as child abuse, terrorism, drug trafficking, human trafficking, identity theft, fraud, assassinations and weapons distribution.

divisions.question: The majority voted against a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2020-12-08.127.2) introduced by Victorian Senator [Lidia Thorpe](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/victoria/lidia_thorpe) (Greens), which means it failed. Before voting, Tasmanian Senator [Jonathon Duniam](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/tasmania/jonathon_duniam) (Liberal) [noted that](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2020-12-08.128.4): > *The government does not support this motion. The Minister for Home Affairs has already written to the chair of the [Parliamentary Joint Standing Committee on Intelligence and Security](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Committees/Joint/Intelligence_and_Security) referring the legislation to the PJCIS as the appropriate committee in this instance.* You can [track the inquiry](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Committees/Joint/Intelligence_and_Security/IdentifyandDisruptBill). ### Motion text > *That the Senate—* > > *(a) notes that the [Surveillance Legislation Amendment (Identify and Disrupt) Bill 2020](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r6623) gives the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission, the Australian Federal Police and, through them, the Australian Signals Directorate extraordinary powers in respect to online activities; and* > > *(b) refers the Surveillance Legislation Amendment (Identify and Disrupt) Bill 2020 to the [Legal and Constitutional Affairs Legislation Committee](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Committees/Senate/Legal_and_Constitutional_Affairs) for inquiry and report by 27 March 2021.*

speeches.speaker: Peter Dutton
speeches.brief: The Surveillance Legislation Amendment (Identify and Disrupt) Bill 2020 creates three new powers for the AFP and ACIC—network activity warrants, data disruption warrants, and account takeover warrants—to combat serious crimes on the dark web and using anonymising technologies. The speech cited that the ACCCE intercepted over 250,000 child abuse material files, resulting in 302 arrests and 229 children removed from harm, while noting a 163% increase in dark web child abuse material downloads from April to June 2020.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Giles
speeches.brief: Labor supported the Surveillance Legislation Amendment (Identify and Disrupt) Bill 2020, which introduces three new warrant types—data disruption, network activity, and account takeover—to help the AFP and ACIC combat serious cybercrime on the dark web. The bill includes safeguards such as oversight by the Ombudsman and Inspector-General, a five-year sunset, and 23 of 33 committee recommendations were implemented, though Labor noted concerns that the powers could apply to offences beyond the most serious crimes.

speeches.speaker: Vince Connelly
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in support of the Surveillance Legislation Amendment (Identify and Disrupt) Bill 2020, which introduces network activity, data disruption and account takeover warrants to combat online crime on the dark web, citing a 163% increase in child abuse material and 696 search warrants, 290 charges and 139 weapons seized via Operation Ironside. The speaker also noted that 39% of federally convicted child-sex offenders previously spent no time in jail.

speeches.speaker: Graham Perrett
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Surveillance Legislation Amendment (Identify and Disrupt) Bill, which grants the AFP and ACIC new online disruption, network activity, and account takeover warrants, but called for all 34 Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security recommendations to be adopted—particularly that issuing authorities for warrants be superior court judges rather than AAT members or magistrates.

speeches.speaker: Celia Hammond
speeches.brief: The Surveillance Legislation Amendment (Identify and Disrupt) Bill 2020 introduces three new powers for the AFP and ACIC: data disruption warrants, network activity warrants, and account takeover warrants, aimed at combating online serious crime. The government accepted 25 of the 33 recommendations made by the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security, and the speaker supported the bill.

speeches.speaker: Tim Watts
speeches.brief: The member argued that while the bill’s new warrant powers for the AFP and ACIC are necessary to combat serious cyber‑enabled crime on the dark web, the government rushed the process and the definition of “relevant offences” should be tightened to a seven‑year imprisonment threshold rather than the current three‑year threshold.

speeches.speaker: Fiona Martin
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Surveillance Legislation Amendment (Identify and Disrupt) Bill 2020, arguing it gives the AFP and ACIC three new powers—network activity warrants, data disruption warrants, and account takeover powers—to fight serious cyber-enabled crime, citing Operation Ironside's outcomes (696 search warrants, 290 charged, $49 million cash seized) and noting amendments strengthen oversight and transparency.

speeches.speaker: Tim Wilson
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Surveillance Legislation Amendment (Identify and Disrupt) Bill 2020 but expressed reservations, highlighting three new powers—network activity warrants, data disruption warrants, and account takeover warrants—for the AFP and ACIC to combat cybercrime, while stressing the need for ongoing oversight and safeguards to maintain public confidence.

speeches.speaker: Patrick Conaghan
speeches.brief: The Surveillance Legislation Amendment (Identify and Disrupt) Bill 2020 is necessary to combat cyber-enabled crime, with the speaker citing operations Arkstone and Ironside as examples of the need for new powers. The bill introduces network activity warrants, data disruption warrants, and account takeover powers to help the AFP and ACIC investigate and disrupt serious crimes including child exploitation, drug trafficking, and extremist content on the dark web.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Wallace
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Surveillance Legislation Amendment (Identify and Disrupt) Bill 2020 is necessary to give the AFP and ACIC new powers to collect online intelligence, take control of criminal accounts, and disrupt data, citing a 163% increase in child abuse material downloads and Operation Ironside's seizure of nearly $50 million and 250 charges. The government’s $1.7 billion Cyber Security Strategy and $6.1 million in additional funding for IDCARE were also highlighted.

speeches.speaker: Karen Andrews
speeches.brief: The government argued the Surveillance Legislation Amendment (Identify and Disrupt) Bill 2020 is vital for equipping the AFP and ACIC to combat serious crime on the dark web, citing Operation Ironside’s arrest of over 220 criminals. An addendum to the explanatory memorandum was circulated, addressing issues raised by three parliamentary committees.
